display_title: Official Review of Paper4093 by Reviewer LwLQ

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an adversarial attack, called uncertainty-targeted attacks (UTA), which utilize the entropy maximization for generating perturbations. The paper combines UTA with PGD for adversarial training. The empirical results show that the models trained by the proposed method are robust to PGD attacks, while keeps high clean accuracy compared to the models trained by adversarial training with PGD.
content.main_review:
The paper proposes an attack method based on entropy maximization. The empirical study shows adversarial training with the proposed method achieves better clean-robust accuracy trade-off compared to adversarial training with PGD.

However, the idea of utilizing entropy maximization for adversarial training is not novel. Moreover, the empirical evaluation via PGD robustness is not sufficient, so more precise evaluations are needed. The details of the concerns are described below:

 The idea of utilizing entropy maximization for adversarial training is not novel. A previous study [1] already exploited entropy maximization for adversarial training. Although the previous study used entropy maximization for regularization, the novelty of this paper is limited.

* The 2D experiment in Figure 1 is intuitive, but I am not convinced this experiment shows the advantage of UTA for two reasons. 1) The setting of this experiment is far from normal settings, because $\epsilon$-ball for a data sample should not contain any other samples. If a sample with a different label is within $\epsilon$-ball, the sample is not “adversarial”. 2) While the purpose of adversarial training is to train robust models, this experiment does not focus on robust accuracy.

* As the authors mentioned, PGD attacks may fall into a local minimum. PGD attacks can also suffer from gradient masking. Actually, in Figure 2-4 and Figure 6, PGD accuracy under $\epsilon=0.5$ sometimes higher than 0.2. These results suggest the evaluation by gradient-based attacks is not sufficient to evaluate the robustness of the proposed defense method properly. Previous studies have mentioned that defense models should be evaluated on adaptive attacks (e.g. [2]). In addition, AutoAttack [3] is a powerful benchmark attack for the evaluation of adversarial robustness, which contains not only gradient-based attacks, but also gradient-free black-box attacks. Unless the models trained by the proposed method are properly evaluated by using these attacks, the empirical comparisons are not sufficient.

* Adversarial training with latent-space attacks under various $\epsilon$ is essentially not meaningful, because the scale of latent space is arbitrary. By multiplying the last layer of the encoder by a constant C and the first layer of the classifier by 1/C, we can change the scale of latent space so that the condition in the optimization problem holds. The trained model with various $\epsilon$ can be different, but it will be not due to the difference of $\epsilon$, but due to optimizer and weight regularization.

Minor comments
* In the definition of PGD in Section 3, $\delta_{PGD}^0=0$. However, $\delta_{PGD}^0$ is typically sampled within a ball like R-FGSM. For example, Madry et al. [4] used a random perturbation as a starting point of PGD for adversarial training.

[1] Yilun Jin, Lixin Fan, Kam Woh Ng, Ce Ju, and Qiang Yang. Rethinking Uncertainty in Deep Learning: Whether and How it Improves Robustness. arxiv 2011.13538.

[2] Florian Tramer, Nicholas Carlini, Wieland Brendel, and Aleksander Madry. On Adaptive Attacks to Adversarial Example Defenses. NeurIPS 2020.

[3] Francesco Croce and Matthias Hein. Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks. ICML 2020.

[4] Aleksander Madry, Aleksandar Makelov, Ludwig Schmidt, Dimitris Tsipras, and Adrian Vladu. Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks. ICLR 2018.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer LwLQ
content.comment:
> The paper proposes an attack method based on entropy maximization. The empirical study shows adversarial training with the proposed method achieves better clean-robust accuracy trade-off compared to adversarial training with PGD.

We would like to clarify that our method relies on uncertainty estimation, and entropy is only one way to implement our approach (see our results with MC Dropout and Gaussian Process, Sec. 5.3 and App. A, and discussion in Sec. 2).

> However, the idea of utilizing entropy maximization for adversarial training is not novel. Moreover, the empirical evaluation via PGD robustness is not sufficient, so more precise evaluations are needed. The details of the concerns are described below: The idea of utilizing entropy maximization for adversarial training is not novel. A previous study [1] already exploited entropy maximization for adversarial training. Although the previous study used entropy maximization for regularization, the novelty of this paper is limited.

We consider using entropy as a regularizer is significantly different from our approach of using uncertainty as an objective when finding the perturbations. Maximizing entropy as a regularizer will maximize the entropy of points sampled from the data distribution. Uncertainty-based AT finds perturbations through maximizing the uncertainty of the model but then minimizes the cross-entropy on those points, it doesn’t attempt to maximize the entropy of perturbations or of points from the data distribution. Moreover, the two approaches can be combined.

> The 2D experiment in Figure 1 is intuitive, but I am not convinced this experiment shows the advantage of UTA for two reasons. 1) The setting of this experiment is far from normal settings, because -ball for a data sample should not contain any other samples. If a sample with a different label is within -ball, the sample is not “adversarial”. 2) While the purpose of adversarial training is to train robust models, this experiment does not focus on robust accuracy.

We clarify our toy example in the *Updated version* comment above. See also Sec. 4.1 and 4.3 in the updated version.  

> As the authors mentioned, PGD attacks may fall into a local minimum. PGD attacks can also suffer from gradient masking. Actually, in Figure 2-4 and Figure 6, PGD accuracy under  sometimes higher than 0.2. These results suggest the evaluation by gradient-based attacks is not sufficient to evaluate the robustness of the proposed defense method properly. Previous studies have mentioned that defense models should be evaluated on adaptive attacks (e.g. [2]). In addition, AutoAttack [3] is a powerful benchmark attack for the evaluation of adversarial robustness, which contains not only gradient-based attacks, but also gradient-free black-box attacks. Unless the models trained by the proposed method are properly evaluated by using these attacks, the empirical comparisons are not sufficient.

We report new results using AutoAttack, please see Table 1.

> Adversarial training with latent-space attacks under various $\epsilon$ is essentially not meaningful, because the scale of latent space is arbitrary. By multiplying the last layer of the encoder by a constant C and the first layer of the classifier by 1/C, we can change the scale of latent space so that the condition in the optimization problem holds. The trained model with various $\epsilon$ can be different, but it will be not due to the difference of $\epsilon$, but due to optimizer and weight regularization.

There is a misunderstanding here, as our method allows for training with somewhat larger $\epsilon$ relative to standard loss-based methods, and thus the reviewer’s argument does not hold. Moreover, in general, the model does not do the rescaling itself so as to ensure the condition holds.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4093 by Reviewer XGNS

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a PGD-like attack for maximizing uncertainty (instead of maximizing cross-entropy loss). They argue that adversarial training with this attacks leads to better clean accuracy and thus a better accuracy-robustness trade-off. Furthermore, it can be applied in latent space and is shown to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The paper is generally well-structured and mostly easy to read and follow; plots are clear; the algorithm helps to understand the method.
- An interesting problem is addressed: the accuracy-robustness trade-off of adversarial training.
- Considering uncertainty instead or in addition to mis-classification seems interesting.
- The 2D example helps to follow the argumentation and is generally a good way to introduce the high-level intuition of the method.
- Experiments on multiple datasets and with latent-space perturbations.

Weaknesses:
- A comment on the introduction: while catastrophic overfitting is severe for few-step attacks, robust overfitting as introduced and discussed in [a,b,c] is generally more severe and important for state-of-the-art adversarial training, in my opinion. I think a brief mention/discussion would benefit the paper.

[a] https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.11569
[b] https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04448
[c] https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05884

- There are actually papers that also do a type of adversarial training with attacks motivated through uncertainty. [d] does this for out-of-distribution detection, [e] does it for robustness against various threat models and references in [e] include other examples.

[d] https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05720
[e] https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06259

- The related work part on adversarial training is very superficial in my opinion. The problem is that there is a large body of work on adversarial training and I would expect the authors to make an effort to discuss and differentiate from similar approaches, some mentioned above. Also, the current state-of-the-art does not become clear and is not compared against in experiments later. [b,e,f,g] contain recent discussions of work on adversarial training that the authors could check which works are relevant to include/discuss.

[f] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00467
[g] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03593

- While I like the idea of having a 2D example as illustration, I see an important flaw: In the introduction, the authors specifically highlight that the perturbation has to be chosen in away ensuring label invariance. However, assuming that the background colors show the ground truth decision boundary, this is not ensured in this example. For the 20 steps attack for standard AT it directly becomes clear that all adversarial examples went “to the other side” of the decision boundary. This means that these are NOT adversarial examples – they truly changed to an extent that the true label changes. This was actually discussed in the context of the paper by Tsipras et al. in the appendix of Stutz et al., making exactly the same point. The important part here is to acknowledge that if the true class, considering the true posterior distribution, changes within the epsilon-ball, then these are not “adversarial” examples. The analogy on images would be if we allow the attacker to change a dog image to a cat image and humans do really recognize it as a cat (without doubt). This also questions the motivation of the approach, because it seems that UTA mainly preserves clean accuracy because it does not exploit the full epsilon-ball by stopping at the true decision boundary which is estimated based on uncertainty. This could also be achieved using instance-adaptive epsilon-balls as proposed in some papers for adversarial training or just ensuring that the epsilon ball is chosen in a way that they do not overlap between examples of different classes.
- Regarding to the discussion above, I would be interested in seeing the average perturbation obtained by the attack at test time compared to standard PGD to see if UTA mainly improves clean accuracy by resulting in "weaker" adversarial examples in terms of perturbation size.
- The experiments miss important baselines. As the main goal is to allow a better robustness-accuracy trade-off, the most trivial baseline would be adversarial training with X% adversarial examples and 100-X% clean examples. Varying X allows to control the trade-off as described in Stutz et al. Also, more recent adversarial training baselines (TRADES [h], AT-AWP [c], etc.) are missing and it is unclear whether early stopping was employed.

[h] https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08573

- The attack evaluation at test time is too weak. PGD is used, probably without any random restarts. I would expect at least an ensemble of multiple attacks or PGD with multiple restarts and more iterations. Ideally, us a standard benchmark such as AutoAttack [i]. Thus, the robustness results are not very reliable. In any case, Fig. 2 shows that standard AT outperforms UTA-AT significantly in terms of robustness, so the remaining benefit would be better clean accuracy for especially high epsilon-ball.

[i] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.01690.pdf

- Side comment: epsilon-balls for L_inf of 0.5 or above do not make sense for MNIST or Fashion-MNIST as the class label cannot be presered (the image can become completely gray).
- For SVHN, some epsilon values in between 0.01 and 0.05 would be interesting, like 8/255 as on CIFAR10.
- Regarding the latent-space attacks: how is it ensured that the true label of the perturbed representation does not change? Stutz et al. Use a class-specific generative model to ensure that, but here rather large L_inf epsilon-balls of up to 0.5 are used which seems too large.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I do not think that this paper is ready for ICLR. The main reasons for this assessment are the flaws in terms of the 2D illustration (and thereby the motivation) and insufficient experimental results (missing simple baselines, unreliable robustness evaluation at test time, non-standard, sometimes not meaningful hyper-parameters/threat models).

content.title: Reply to Reviewer XGNS: Part 2/2
content.comment:
> Regarding to the discussion above, I would be interested in seeing the average perturbation obtained by the attack at test time compared to standard PGD to see if UTA mainly improves clean accuracy by resulting in "weaker" adversarial examples in terms of perturbation size.

Indeed, in this work, we do not focus on finding strong test-time attacks, and the fact that UTA does not cross the decision boundary makes it a less strong attack relative to loss-based attacks. However, we do show that uncertainty-based adversarial training yet achieves a *better* robustness-generalization tradeoff. In fact, our work demonstrates that the “most effective” perturbations in terms of best generalization-robustness trade-offs are not necessarily the ones to achieve the highest adversarial robustness.
 
We agree with the reviewer that one can exploit the advantage of UTA to find “locally adaptive” $\epsilon$ (upper bounded by a given value) and moreover combine it with enforcing to cross the boundary, which is out of scope in this paper, and we leave it for future work. 
 
> The experiments miss important baselines. As the main goal is to allow a better robustness-accuracy trade-off, the most trivial baseline would be adversarial training with X% adversarial examples and 100-X% clean examples. Varying X allows to control the trade-off as described in Stutz et al. Also, more recent adversarial training baselines (TRADES [h], AT-AWP [c], etc.) are missing and it is unclear whether early stopping was employed. [h] https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08573

As part of our experiments, we did mixed training with 50% clean and 50% adversarial perturbations. However, this did not give significantly different results, and in particular, it does not prevent the failure of loss-based AT for large training epsilons. We added TRADES in our related work section as well as an experiment applying TRADES to our toy example, we observe that TRADES suffers from the same problem as PGD-AT by failing to cope with larger epsilons, please see Sec.2 and Fig. 8 in the updated version.
> The attack evaluation at test time is too weak. PGD is used, probably without any random restarts. I would expect at least an ensemble of multiple attacks or PGD with multiple restarts and more iterations. Ideally, us a standard benchmark such as AutoAttack [i]. Thus, the robustness results are not very reliable. 

We added new results with AutoAttack, please see Table 1. Our conclusions remain unchanged in that uncertainty-based AT consistently brings better trade-offs relative to loss-based AT.

> In any case, Fig. 2 shows that standard AT outperforms UTA-AT significantly in terms of robustness, so the remaining benefit would be better clean accuracy for especially high epsilon-ball.  [i] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.01690.pdf

One of the key messages that we point out is that by using larger $\epsilon_{larger}$ one is often more robust to smaller $\epsilon_{smaller}< \epsilon_{larger}$ values at test time, relative to training with loss-based AT with $\epsilon_{smaller}$ (while also achieving better generalization). Please see the results Tab. 1 of the updated version where we point this more explicitly. 

> Side comment: epsilon-balls for L_inf of 0.5 or above do not make sense for MNIST or Fashion-MNIST as the class label cannot be presered (the image can become completely gray). For SVHN, some epsilon values in between 0.01 and 0.05 would be interesting, like 8/255 as on CIFAR10.

Indeed, as we noted in the main paper, we have added the results for $\epsilon_{test} = 0.5$ for MNIST as a sanity check (and we do get close to 0 robustness, and as the problem is non-convex one cannot expect exactly 0). See Tab. 1 for new results for SVHN.

> Regarding the latent-space attacks: how is it ensured that the true label of the perturbed representation does not change? Stutz et al. Use a class-specific generative model to ensure that, but here rather large L_inf epsilon-balls of up to 0.5 are used which seems too large.

In practice, similarly as in image-space, one can exactly find $\epsilon$ for which AT-Asm is not broken when adding the perturbations in the latent space. We do not use class-specific generative model, but rather add perturbations in the latent space of the model itself as in [Yuksel et al., 2021].

I appreciate the authors comments and answers.

I am surprised that 50%/50% training did not result in a better trade-off for the authors, while this has been reproduced in several papers as far as I am aware.

Overall, I think I do not change my opinion about the paper. While several of the changes are definitely in the right direction, I do not think the paper is ready for ICLR yet.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer XGNS: Part 1/2
content.comment:
> A comment on the introduction: while catastrophic overfitting is severe for few-step attacks, robust overfitting as introduced and discussed in [a,b,c] is generally more severe and important for state-of-the-art adversarial training, in my opinion. I think a brief mention/discussion would benefit the paper.
[a] https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.11569 [b] https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04448 [c] https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05884

Thanks for the suggestion, we will include a short discussion on it, however, we do not consider it very relevant, due to the following. Robust overfitting refers to the case when the robust training loss keeps decreasing while at a certain point the robust test loss starts increasing. While low clean accuracy implies low robust accuracy, the reverse does not hold. In this work, we focus in large part on the problem of low clean accuracy of loss-based AT.

> There are actually papers that also do a type of adversarial training with attacks motivated through uncertainty. [d] does this for out-of-distribution detection, [e] does it for robustness against various threat models and references in [e] include other examples.
[d] https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05720 [e] https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06259

Thanks for the references, we will include a discussion on why these are different from our approach.

While [d] tries to push the model to have high uncertainty estimates for OOD samples, our method uses the uncertainty estimates to *find* perturbations which maximize it, and thus the two methods are orthogonal in the sense that these can be combined. 

Interestingly, [e] shares similar intuition with our motivation as it rejects samples with low confidence, thus effectively samples close to the decision boundary. This in turn reduces *to some extend* crossing the decision boundary. On the other hand, our uncertainty-based AT method achieves this more "elegantly", and retains the data points instead of rejecting these and thus has an advantage to further improve the generalization.
   
> The related work part on adversarial training is very superficial in my opinion. The problem is that there is a large body of work on adversarial training and I would expect the authors to make an effort to discuss and differentiate from similar approaches, some mentioned above. Also, the current state-of-the-art does not become clear and is not compared against in experiments later. [b,e,f,g] contain recent discussions of work on adversarial training that the authors could check which works are relevant to include/discuss.
[f] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00467 [g] https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03593

Indeed, there exist a handful of AT methods. However, this work proposes replacing the standard loss objective when finding the perturbation with the model’s estimated uncertainty. As such, many of the existing methods can be combined with ours, what limits their relevance in the interest of keeping the discussion on point. However, we have updated our related work section--please see Sec. 2--with works that share similar intuition as our motivation, and we will add the above references as well.

> While I like the idea of having a 2D example as illustration, I see an important flaw: In the introduction, the authors specifically highlight that the perturbation has to be chosen in away ensuring label invariance. [...]

Please see the section on the toy example in the *Updated version* comment above. 

In short, indeed we write AT-Asm explicitly to emphasize that standard AT methods in cases where the locally optimal $\epsilon$ values differ notably--such as the toy-example--would choose the smallest $\epsilon$, as otherwise, they perform poorly. So, indeed, it is very unlikely that a practitioner would choose such value for loss-based AT. However, we point out that this approach has disadvantages: it reduces the effectiveness of AT as some datasets (and not necessarily image datasets) can have negligible $\epsilon$ that does not break AT, and other datasets can have a large difference between the locally optimal $\epsilon$ values (thus the robustness will *not* be sufficiently improved in the regions where the $\epsilon$ values *can* be larger). Finally, by "relaxing" this assumption (or more precisely using locally-adaptive $\epsilon$) we do achieve a better trade-off. Please see our comment above and the updated Sec. 4.1 and 4.3. Please let us know if this clarifies the motivation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work the authors propose an alternative to the often used adversarial training defence against adversarial examples. The proposed defence strategy moves away from the traditional loss-based view towards one focussed on the uncertainty of the model. By focussing on areas of low uncertainty instead of areas of high loss during the adversarial training step the method is capable of exploring further away from the original starting sample.
content.main_review:
Please find below my review of the paper *Improved Generalization-Robustness Trade-off via Uncertainty Targeted Attacks*. While I do believe the paper to have its merits, I can unfortunately not recommend the current manuscript to be accepted for publication at the ICLR conference. My main reason for this is that I do not believe the proposed defence strategy to be in line with the intentions of an adversary attacking a model. I will discuss this further below. In addition to this, the experimental evaluation is in my opinion not in depth enough.

### Alignment between defence and intentions of the adversary

As far as I understood, the main advantage of using an uncertainty-targeted attack over a tradition loss based attack is its functionality to also explore areas away from the decision border that have low uncertainty. While the study of low confidence areas is in itself an interesting domain in the context of generalisation, I fail to understand the relevance of studying these areas in the context of adversarial robustness. Considering the side of the adversary, these areas of low uncertainty are not of interest as they do not change the prediction of the system. Hence, by exploring these areas during the adversarial training process one does not influence the capacity of the model to defend against adversarial examples generated by an adversary. 

Additionally, while areas of low uncertainty are of interest in the context of generalisation, I do not believe that artificially raising the certainty of the model in these areas by adversarial training is desirable. This implicitly assumes that we wish the model to have a high certainty for unnaturally perturbed data. 

### Experimental evaluation

While I admire the authors extensive study using multiple dataset, multiple models, and multiple train/test epsilons, I still believe the experimental evaluation to be incomplete. Specifically, the experimental evaluation should have contained a study of the performance of the defence strategy using an adaptive attack focussed on exploiting the uncertainty aspect of the model. Using an adaptive attack should in general always be part of the evaluation of any defence strategy. 

Related to this, I also believe that the trade-off between robustness generalisation should have been explored further (both theoretically and empirically) given the emphasis placed on this in the title of the paper.

### Small Notes

- The view of robustness and generalisation as being opposing goals presented in the introduction is in my opinion too one-sided. Also discussing the opposing view in this section (as for example discussed in [Stutz, 2019]) would provide a more complete overview.
- The related work sections gives the impression that it was primarily an afterthought written when the paper was already completed. In my opinion it does not successfully place the contributions of the paper in the context of the wider body of literature. The section on uncertainty estimation not discussing prior work on studying BNNs in the context of adversarial examples is a clear example of this.
- Last line before Fig. 1 needs a space before "See"
- Description of Fig. 1 needs a cleanup. For example, it mentions twice that the top is PGD and the bottom UTA. Once at the start and once when discussing col. c.

My main reason for this is that I do not believe the proposed defence strategy to be in line with the intentions of an adversary attacking a model. I will discuss this further below. In addition to this, the experimental evaluation is in my opinion not in depth enough.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer mAmo
content.comment:
Thanks for the insightful comments and elaborated justification. We updated the version and below we reference the relevant updated parts of the paper. As a reminder, we denote with $\epsilon$ the size of the ball selected to perform the data-point perturbations.

> [...] While the study of low confidence areas is in itself an interesting domain in the context of generalisation, I fail to understand the relevance of studying these areas in the context of adversarial robustness. Considering the side of the adversary, these areas of low uncertainty are not of interest as they do not change the prediction of the system. Hence, by exploring these areas during the adversarial training process one does not influence the capacity of the model to defend against adversarial examples generated by an adversary.

Indeed, we agree that our method is largely motivated from a generalization perspective relative, yet the two are related: AT will not have an impact on a model that generalizes well/perfectly. We make a simple argument in the paper which is based on these two considerations:  
(1) maximum margin implies improved generalization (Vapnik, 2000) 
(2) AT with $\epsilon_{tr}$ ensures the boundary lies within a margin that is far by at least $\epsilon_{tr}/2$ from any training data point. 
The argument is as follows: 
- It is reasonable to assume that the largest $\epsilon$ values which do not break the assumption of Eq. (AT-Asm) in the paper *locally* would in general *differ* amongst the $m$ non-overlapping local regions -- as in our toy-example, and let us denote these with $\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, \dots, \epsilon_m$ and as such none of these $\epsilon_i$ when applied to its own local region $i$ changes the label class. Let without loss of generality $\epsilon_1 < \epsilon_2< \dots < \epsilon_m$. AT-Asm forces that for training we select $\epsilon^{tr} = min(\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, \dots , \epsilon_m) = \epsilon_1$. In all the regions apart from region $1$ we can not guarantee that the margin is maximized. On the contrary, using the corresponding $\epsilon_i$ for region $i$ will ensure the margin is larger (ideally maximized). 

We updated the paper to include this argument, please see Sec. 4.3, and thanks a lot for the question.

Moreover, this relationship is empirically motivated in the opposite direction: uncertainty-based AT achieves both good **loss**-based robustness (used *solely* at test-time) and notably larger generalization accuracy (relative to loss-based AT training)--in turn, a better trade-off. 

> Additionally, while areas of low uncertainty are of interest in the context of generalisation, I do not believe that artificially raising the certainty of the model in these areas by adversarial training is desirable. This implicitly assumes that we wish the model to have a high certainty for unnaturally perturbed data.

We would like to first clarify that *loss*-based AT with $\epsilon$ that does *not* violate (AT-Asm):  *(i)* (also) “artificially decreases” the uncertainty around the data points, and *(ii)* if AT-Asm indeed holds (the label $y$ is the true label in any point in the $\epsilon$-ball around $x$), then there is no motive why the uncertainty should be high in the $\epsilon$-ball around that data point. Or in other words, the reviewer’s comment applies also to any AT method. If a data-input region is “visited” from training data points from the same class, indeed the uncertainty will be reduced. And likewise, if such a region is visited “from” different class data points the uncertainty will be high.

> While I admire the authors extensive study using multiple dataset, multiple models, and multiple train/test epsilons, I still believe the experimental evaluation to be incomplete. Specifically, the experimental evaluation should have contained a study of the performance of the defence strategy using an adaptive attack focussed on exploiting the uncertainty aspect of the model. Using an adaptive attack should in general always be part of the evaluation of any defence strategy.

We updated our results to use the standard pipeline of AutoAttack, for both our image-space and latent-space experiments, please see Table 1 and 2. We observe that the improvement relative to loss-based training is consistent when evaluating with AutoAttack as well.

> Related to this, I also believe that the trade-off between robustness generalisation should have been explored further (both theoretically and empirically) given the emphasis placed on this in the title of the paper.

Thanks for the suggestion. To show the trade-off between robustness and generalization and simplify the interpretation of the results, we reported in Tables 1 and 2 the average between the robustness accuracy (from AutoAttack) and the clean accuracy.

- Regarding the new motivation for using UTA as described in section 4.3. Unfortunately, the late response leaves me with insufficient time to carefully evaluate this important new claim. However, based on my first instinct, I do not fully agree with the authors line of reason here. I do not believe that the presented UTA defence increased the maximum sample margin of the model. The larger $\epsilon_{train}$ of UTA is effectively only used in areas away from the decision boundary and therefore has no real effect on it. Again, I unfortunately do not have time to make this counterpoint more factual. 

- Regarding the point on artificially reducing the uncertainty. The main difference in this case between AT and UTA is that UTA is motivated by the assumption that we should raise the uncertainty of unnaturally perturbed samples while AT is only motivated by the assumption that the unnaturally perturbed samples should have the same classification. In other words, for AT it is perfectly reasonable if the uncertainty of a perturbed sample is very low as long as it is classified similar to the natural sample. 

- While auto attack is a great evaluation method for adversarial defences, I do not believe it to be a replacement for an adaptive attack. An adaptive attack evaluation is crucial for showing that the authors have considered all possible failure cases of their method and have communicated these clearly. 

- I do not see how the presented averaged accuracy over clean and adversarial examples studies the robustness-generalisation trade off.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes training l-infinity adversarially robust models by training against an attack that maximizes the entropy of the model's prediction.
content.main_review:
In terms of language, formatting and general presentation, the paper is well written. For as minor improvement, I would suggest to try to streamline the Experiments section by not having a new figure with caption for each dataset.

Figure 1 does not depict the situation that is usually assumed when adversarial attacks are considered. The standard classifier in (a) and (b) separates the classes well, and the samples in (b-top) are not adversarial examples as the semantic properties have actually been changed: e.g. many of the blue perturbed pluses are close to (and could have been chosen exactly at) red circles. In other words, if the second condition of AT-Asm is not fulfilled for an \tilde{x}, it is not an adversarial example. It would be better to have an example where the standard classifier is not robust, e.g. by having a zig-zag-y decision boundary. So this example shows that UTA might be better than AT when standard training already produces almost ideal models, which is also reflected in the observation that the shown UTA prediction (c-bottom) are hardly different from those of the standard model (a-top, b-top).

The paper confuses attacks and training against attacks in many places. For example, Eq. (UTA) describes training with the attack. A discussion of the attack itself before using it in training would be useful.

"Finally, relative to standard AT methods, UTA: (i) is unsupervised": If UTA means training with the first row of Eq. (UTA), the labels are used! If it just means the attack, it does indeed not use labels, but can't be compared to AT, which is a training scheme.
Anyway, this paper should also compare to TRADES (Zhang et al., ICML'19, https://github.com/yaodongyu/TRADES), which is widely used and consistently shows at least slight improvements over AT. TRADES can be described as 'unsupervised' in this sense, since the attack and defense do not use labels but predictions. TRADES is very important for the context of this paper, but also the newer state-of-the-art adversarial defenses need to be discussed.

It is not clear why the paper emphasizes the distinction between single model and ensemble, when in (E), it uses the entropy of the mean prediction of the potential (if M>1) ensemble for the quantification of the uncertainty. Some methods that use variance within the ensemble (or dropout predictions) are cited, but this does not have anything to do with what this paper does.


The evaluations are too superficial. For evaluating adversarial robustness, only PGD is used, which is not acceptable for a paper discussing adversarial robustness in 2021. At least, some state of the art attack should be run on the models, for example for MNIST strong ones from https://github.com/MadryLab/mnist_challenge, and for CIFAR https://robustbench.github.io/. Also, the paper should describe reasonably thinkable adapted attacks that target potential specific weaknesses of the proposed defense.
Proposed defenses must also be compared to previous state-of-the-art defenses, not just to AT. For MNIST: https://github.com/fra31/auto-attack#mnist---linf ; the models there are all much stronger than what this paper shows, with an adversarial robustness at $\epsilon = 0.3$ of above 96%, compared to this paper's below 50% in Figure 4. For CIFAR-10:https://robustbench.github.io/ . 

Showing (weak) evaluations on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and SVHN is not enough for modern adversarial defenses. A full evaluation on CIFAR-10, which would be the most interesting dataset in this paper, is unexplainedly left out, and only results for fast attacks during training are shown.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The evaluations are far too shallow in terms of shown datasets, used attacks, and compared methods, such that it is not possible to conclude that the propose method works at all, much less reasonable well, to achieve adversarial robustness. The method itself and the theoretical considerations are not very intriguing, with the supporting toy example not being insightful as it describes a data situation that does not align with the usual definition of adversarial vulnerability.

####################################

## Update:

Most of the rather large number of original concerns have been resolved, most importantly the evaluation attacks now use AutoAttack instead of basic PGD. Some minor points can still be improved (see the three comment threads below) and better comparisons to other methods that have the same performance goals are necessary.

Most importantly, paper is still missing evaluation in the standard adversarial training setting on CIFAR-10, which is necessary for the reader to judge the proposed method in the most well-studied setting.

Thus I still rather recommend to reject the paper (score raised from 1 to 5).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 3/3
content.comment:
# Comments on the empirical evaluation 

> [...] but also the newer state-of-the-art adversarial defenses need to be discussed. [..] The evaluations are too superficial. For evaluating adversarial robustness, only PGD is used, which is not acceptable for a paper discussing adversarial robustness in 2021.
We respectfully disagree with the reviewer, and there is a misunderstanding of our contributions.

This work does *not* propose a new way of “moving” in the $\epsilon$  ball but rather changes the objective when doing so. This discards the relevance to discuss (and compare “against”) to a large number of loss-based AT methods as many of these can be combined with UTA. More precisely, AT methods differ in how the inner expectation of AT is implemented, thus the same method can be used for UTA.

> Summary Of The Review: The evaluations are far too shallow in terms of shown datasets, used attacks, and compared methods, such that it is not possible to conclude that the propose method works at all, much less reasonable well, to achieve adversarial robustness. 

The relevant question our evaluation addresses is: “*For a fixed setup, does using the uncertainty estimate as an objective yield as good or often better performance to that when using the loss as an objective?*” 
To address the above question we vary:
- 2 types of training attacks, and 4 types of test attacks (see updated version with AutoAttack), 
- 3 different models, 
- 4 datasets, 
- 3 different uncertainty methods and 
- 2 different attack spaces (latent and input-space). 

Our extensive empirical evaluation answers affirmatively, and we consider our findings could be relevant/helpful for the ICLR community.

> At least, some state of the art attack should be run on the models, for example for MNIST strong ones from https://github.com/MadryLab/mnist_challenge, and for CIFAR https://robustbench.github.io/. 

See our revised version where we observe that the improvement is *consistent* with PGD/FGSM  when using AutoAttack.

> Also, the paper should describe reasonably thinkable adapted attacks that target potential specific weaknesses of the proposed defense. Proposed defenses must also be compared to previous state-of-the-art defenses, not just to AT. For MNIST: https://github.com/fra31/auto-attack#mnist---linf ; the models there are all much stronger than what this paper shows, with an adversarial robustness at  of above 96%, compared to this paper's below 50% in Figure 4. For CIFAR-10:https://robustbench.github.io/. [...] Showing (weak) evaluations on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and SVHN is not enough for modern adversarial defenses. A full evaluation on CIFAR-10, which would be the most interesting dataset in this paper, is unexplainedly left out, and only results for fast attacks during training are shown.

- This paper does **not** aim to provide new state of art results in adversarial robustness. 
- Rather than using the loss as an objective when finding adversarial examples, we propose to use the estimated uncertainty of the model. 
- As such *any* loss-based AT method which proposes specific way to traverse the $\epsilon$ ball *can* also be used with uncertainty-based AT. In other words, uncertainty can be combined with many of the existing methods.

This clarification emphasizes that we do not need to compare against all existing methods, but it rather suffices to show that for a fixed setup uncertainty-based AT outperforms loss-based AT, and we moreover show that this is consistent for various attacks, datasets, models, etc. (see the comment above). Note that in the updated version we added AutoAttack results (see our update summary comment above).

replying_to: Replying to Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 3/3

content.title: Answer to Part 3/3
content.comment:
The goal of the method is to train better models, concretely to improve the adversarial robustness - clean accuracy trade-off.
This means it is important to compare with other approaches that aim for that same goal.
I understand that the authors say that for AT, using uncertainty instead of the classification CE leads to improvements.
While this is insightful, there are other methods that improve AT.
They implement things differently compared to AT, but they provide solutions/improvements to the same problem.
Therefore they should be compared to.
If the same methods can be used with UTA, that does not mean that the original versions of these methods cannot be compared to UTA. 
Rather, it would be great (not necessary, but a strong point for UTA) to see if they can be used together.
If other published methods perform better than UTA in certain situations, the reader should be informed about that.
I do not expect UTA to beat every other method as a hard prerequisite for acceptance, but for context some recent SOTA solutions to the same problem of robustness-accuracy tradeoff should be provided.

The inclusion of AutoAttack is very welcome and resolves my concerns on the evaluation of adversarial robustness. Potentially there might still be clever adaptive attacks that make use of the knowledge that the model was trained with UTA, but I don't see concerning properties induced by UTA compared to AT that might make AutoAttack not find exisiting adversarials, so it should be fine.

The contributions, apart from showing that a toy dataset where UTA is better than loss-AT and stating that a new method is proposed and the avoidance of catastrophic overfitting in Fast-AT, mention:
* "*do not drastically decrease the clean test accuracy relative to PGD*" -> is the goal not rather *do not drastically decrease the clean test accuracy relative to clean* and *improve the clean test accuracy relative to PGD*, since the experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and SVHN show *better* clean test accuracy relative to PGD?
* "*it is robust to PGD attacks*" -> this would be quite weak and uninteresting (see original review), but now it could be updated to "it is robust to adversarial attacks" since AutoAttack is the standard?

My technical concerns (both regarding theory and adversarial evaluation) are mostly resolved. The tables and figures experimental section are better organized in the updated version.

However, experiments with CIFAR-10, the most important (besides ImageNet) dataset in the robustness community are still mostly missing.
Standard AT has been used relatively successfully on CIFAR-10 for a long time, and most other methods have been reported for CIFAR.
While the above comment mentions that the quantity of evaluations is large enough, if the authors do not want to include a larger number of results, I suggest replacing Fashion-MNIST with providing all numbers for CIFAR-10.

It would be ok to have results as in Table 1 with proper (non-fast) AT on CIFAR-10 with PGD and UTA even if they were slightly worse for UTA, so the reader knows it is beneficial for some datasets only (the ones shown so far).
But not providing evaluations for the case that is most interesting for most of the community is the main reason why I still recommend rejection (raised from 1 to 5).
While not necessary, including results for CIFAR-100 or ImageNet would also be beneficial.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 2/3
content.comment:
# Comments on the method itself

> The paper confuses attacks and training against attacks in many places. For example, Eq. (UTA) describes training with the attack. A discussion of the attack itself before using it in training would be useful.

There is a misunderstanding here: UTA is not an attack. UTA refers to a *framework*, in a sense that many of the existing adversarial training methods can be implemented with UTA, *e.g.* UTA-PGD, UTA-FGSM, etc. Eq. (UTA) makes this precise. Indeed, other names could have been chosen, however, we chose “UTA” as it is simpler to pronounce. Thus, “UTA” *everywhere* in the paper refers to Uncertainty-based AT, in contrast to loss-based AT. Note that in this work we focus solely on adversarial *training* with perturbed samples and we are not interested in designing a “test-time” attack. 

> "Finally, relative to standard AT methods, UTA: (i) is unsupervised": If UTA means training with the first row of Eq. (UTA), the labels are used! If it just means the attack, it does indeed not use labels, but can't be compared to AT, which is a training scheme. 

If the model to train is supervised, training with perturbed samples requires access to the labels, and Eq. (UTA) is written to contrast it to Eq. AT. We chose this writing as it is common in the literature to include the empirical risk minimization (line one of UTA)--which we consider is evident. However, the second row of (UTA) clearly does not use the label. 

> Anyway, this paper should also compare to TRADES (Zhang et al., ICML'19), which is widely used and consistently shows at least slight improvements over AT. TRADES can be described as 'unsupervised' in this sense, since the attack and defense do not use labels but predictions. TRADES is very important for the context of this paper, [...]

Thanks for the recommendation. We included TRADES in related works and added an experiment with it on the 2D toy example, see Fig. 8 and App. C.1.  

Although TRADES is similar to UTA as it is also unsupervised, it is yet *orthogonal* to our approach in the following sense:
- Assuming the model fits well the training data, effectively the objective to find the perturbed sample x’ given datapoint x is similar to that of loss-based AT: maximizing Loss(f(x’), f(x)) instead of Loss(f(x’), y). For a trained classifier for which f(x’) \approx y, the two would find similar x’. 
- Informally, its main difference is that it enforces the output to be “smoother” with the added regularizer to train the model with, and the authors show that this improves the performances.
- Finally, as UTA only finds x’ in a different way, TRADES can be extended further to UTA as well by using the uncertainty objective to find x’ and training the model with the added regularizer, thus the two approaches are orthogonal.

> It is not clear why the paper emphasizes the distinction between single model and ensemble, when in (E), it uses the entropy of the mean prediction of the potential (if M>1) ensemble for the quantification of the uncertainty. Some methods that use variance within the ensemble (or dropout predictions) are cited, but this does not have anything to do with what this paper does.

The answer behind this question is in fact the core of our paper: the entropy of the mean distribution is one way among many others to estimate the model’s uncertainty, others include: variance, Gaussian Process (GP), BNNs, etc. 
 
These methods are very relevant due to the following:
- Simply put, in this work we propose to change the objective when finding the most efficient perturbation, in particular instead of using the loss we propose to use the *uncertainty estimate* of the model.
- There exist a handful of methods to estimate the uncertainty of the model, entropy being one among these. Monte Carlo-Dropout is one commonly used method to estimate uncertainty (see our cited references). We show that our method outperforms the loss-based baseline even when using a single model, which makes it competitive in terms of computational time with *e.g.* loss-based PGD. 
- *Any* uncertainty estimation method can be used -- thus the relevance. In App. A we show that UTA works better than loss-based PGD when using GP as well, where GPs are popular uncertainty estimation methods. 

This is pointed out on several occasions in the paper, see for example: (1) Sec 3 where we refer to this literature review, and we say that MC Dropout is just an example way of estimating uncertainty, (2) we use MC-Dropout in Sec 5.3 as an example that other uncertainty estimation methods can be used, or (3) our concluding discussion.
 
In summary, since we propose to use uncertainty estimation as an objective to find perturbations, uncertainty estimation methods are very much relevant as these provide means to do so.

> The method itself and the theoretical considerations are not very intriguing,

We hope the reviewer would consider that this is a relative comment, and we disagree.

replying_to: Replying to Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 2/3

content.title: Answer to Part 2/3
content.comment:
I would recommend "uncertainty-targeted attacks" to actually refer to the attacks that are carried out in the inner optimization, and maybe to use something along the lines of "uncertainty-targeted adversarial training" for the framework. Later on, PGD-AT vs. UTA-AT is also not entirely precise, since UTA incorporates projected gradient descent. By the way, is setting number of steps as $\epsilon$ divided by the step size (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST setups) sensible? This means multi-step FGSM, since no projections can happen, and for example $\alpha = 2\epsilon/K$ would be a more common choice.

It is good that TRADES is now included in the discussion and the stated differences and advantages of UTA compared to TRADES are made clear. Particularly the failure of TRADES on the toy example in Figure 7 is a strong addition.
I can see how methodologically, the ideas of TRADES and UTA can be described as orthogonal, however their goals are quite similar, in aiming for adversarial robustness with relatively well preserved clean accuracy. Thus it should also be included in the evaluations, and if it indeed works also the mentioned extension TRADES-UTA.

Could you elaborate how MC Dropout is used in 5.3? Particularly the attack objective is not clear to me from App. B. If I interpret Sec. 3 correctly, the used uncertainty is the entropy of the class prediction, i.e. the same number as for a single model. This means that the paper uses the same method, class prediction entropy, throughout, except for the toy example in App. A.
If this is the case, it should be mentioned that the other techniques only presumably work in practise, since explicit uncertainty estimation techniques that do not rely on standard outputs might behave very differently. On the other hand, it would be very strong (but not necessary) to include experiments that use and maximize such 'external' estimated uncertainties.
If an actually different uncertainty estimation technique is used, please point it out and potentially clarify the process in the paper.

After the updates, I see the UTA training framework as a potentially beneficial idea, but also not as clearly inherently better than other methods like AT/TRADES for real datasets with actual adversarial examples. The main weakness in the logic for why it should be better is that AT-Asm is not 100% *necessary* for AT, which means that ameliorating the problems with AT-Asm is not necessarily 100% beneficial. There are good arguments for it, but its not convincing enough that the theory can stand completely by itself.
Thus in my opinion the theoretical motivations are now fine, but not conclusive by themselves, and hence thorough experimental results that show the consistent benefits of UTA are very necessary to prove the value of the method.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 1/3
content.comment:
Based on the reviewer’s summary and comments (see below where we answer each comment separately) we would like to point out that the reviewer has in large part misunderstood our writeup and all the contributions. We take his/her comments into consideration in the updated version by making some of our discussions more explicit than the original version.

---
# Comments about Figure 1

> Figure 1 does not depict the situation that is usually assumed when adversarial attacks are considered. 

Quoting our contribution one, we explain that: “[..] in particular PGD requires careful tuning of the size of the $\epsilon$-ball, as large $\epsilon$ values *can* break the AT-Asm assumption, and in turn cause oscillations throughout training, see § 4.1.”
Thus, *Fig. 1 is* **not** *intended to show usually assumed situation* but it rather questions the limitations of this assumption in some datasets, please see the first section in our comment above named *Updated version*. 

> The standard classifier in (a) and (b) separates the classes well, 

We are not sure why this is pointed out by Reviewer g8mT. Or in other words, the training loss is often close to zero for deep neural networks as well. 

> and the samples in (b-top) are not adversarial examples as the semantic properties have actually been changed: e.g. many of the blue perturbed pluses are close to (and could have been chosen exactly at) red circles. In other words, if the second condition of AT-Asm is not fulfilled for an \tilde{x}, it is not an adversarial example. 

Yes indeed, this *is* the main reason why we list AT-Asm so explicitly -- so that we can point out that this assumption forces us to choose the *smallest* $\epsilon$ value across the input data space. Please see the first section in our comment above named *Updated version* for clarification. 

>It would be better to have an example where the standard classifier is not robust, e.g. by having a zig-zag-y decision boundary. So this example shows that UTA might be better than AT when standard training already produces almost ideal models, which is also reflected in the observation that the shown UTA prediction (c-bottom) are hardly different from those of the standard model (a-top, b-top). […] with the supporting toy example not being insightful as it describes a data situation that does not align with the usual definition of adversarial vulnerability.

The given toy-example challenges the AT-Asm, in a sense that there could exist datasets where this assumption forces us to choose very small $\epsilon$ value and in turn have only negligible improvement of adversarial training. Please see our *Updated version* comment above, and updated sections 4.1 and 4.3, as there is a big misunderstanding here.

replying_to: Replying to Reply to Reviewer g8mT, Part 1/3

content.title: Answer to Part 1/3
content.comment:
Thanks for clearing up the intention of Fig. 1. To make sure there is no misunderstanding, please correct me if I'm wrong, its main message is: there are potential datasets where loss based AT is detrimental but UTA preserves good performance, particularly for datasets where AT-Asm does not hold.
The reason I pointed out that in the example of Fig. 1 the standard classifier works perfectly and has no real adversarial examples is that in such a case, there would be no need for doing AT or UTA, since one would evaluate the standard classifier and find that it doesn't need to be robustified.
I now see, however, that it can still be valuable to have a method that can be applied in datasets where certain regions look like the data in Fig. 1 and in other regions need some form of adversarial robustification. It would be nice to find a variation of Fig. 1 where UTA is better than both loss based AT and UTA. 

The example in Fig. 1 shows that for datasets where AT-Asm is strongly violated, AT is generally detrimental and one needs something like UTA.
However, as far as I'm aware, papers with AT methods do not make this hard assumption AT-Asm, but rather work relatively well even if a few $x_i$ do not satisfy AT-Asm. Rather than having to choose very small $\epsilon$, standard AT is still done with some $\epsilon$ that allows acceptable results (of course at a trade-of with clean accuracy).
It would be good to cite concrete AT papers that state the AT-Asm, and that mention how they satisfy it, or that discuss why they violate it.

content.title: Updated version
content.comment:
We first discuss the updates relevant to our motivating example from Fig. 1, and we then discuss the added AutoAttack results. We also separately address the reviewers’ comments (see corresponding replies).

---
# Clarification and insights of the toy example in Fig. 1

Our motivating example is to show that the adversarial training assumption (Eq. AT-Asm) for some datasets can be very restrictive: one has to choose the largest $\epsilon$ which does not break (AT-Asm) *globally* across the entire input data space. For some datasets with highly non-isotropic distances between the data points from different classes this requirement can be restrictive: the selected $\epsilon$ value could be negligibly small. Note that, we do **not** claim that *in practice* loss-based PGD methods use $\epsilon$ that breaks (AT-Asm)--see updated Sec. 4.1 where we more explicitly clarify this. However, the goal of Fig. 1 is to contrast its performance with the *uncertainty-based* PGD for such values. 

Uncertainty-based AT (denoted UTA) in a very elegant way deals with non-isotropic distances between the data points from different classes, and thus it is less sensitive to the hyperparameter choice for $\epsilon$, requiring less tuning. And by being able to use larger $\epsilon$ ball it improves the generalization of the model (see updated Sec. 4.3).
Also, we argue that for such datasets, the approach of loss-based AT of choosing $\epsilon$ which does not break AT-Asm, makes AT training limited. This is more evident if one considers different mass-concentrations of the ground-truth probability distribution that generated the dataset: even though there exists a “negligible” region of the input data domain where the local optimal say $\tilde\epsilon \sim 0$ value is much smaller than the rest of the domain, one is restricted to use $\tilde\epsilon$ for training. Moreover, we show empirically that by using larger $\epsilon_{large}$ value for uncertainty-based PGD, one is either *more* robust or *comparably* robust to loss-based PGD *testing* with a smaller $\epsilon_{small}<\epsilon_{large}$, relative to when *training* with that $\epsilon_{small}$ (it also has *improved* clean test accuracy at the same time). In addition, while latent space adversarial perturbations are a common approach for data augmentation, selecting a good $\epsilon$ value is harder in this case. Thus, the above advantage of UTA is particularly useful for latent space perturbations, as our experiments also show.

To summarize, the toy experiment in Fig. 1 is to point out that:
-	Uncertainty-based AT (UTA) has an advantage over loss-based AT of coping well with larger $\epsilon$ values.
-	The inability of loss-based AT to deal with large $\epsilon$ values is not a problem in terms of how adversarial training is commonly expected to work. 
-	However, being able to use somewhat larger $\epsilon$ values improves *generalization* (and thus robustness) what follows from increasing the margin (bringing it closer to the maximum margin).

---
# Added results with AutoAttack

We report new results with a strengthened evaluation using AutoAttack. We also now summarize our results in Table 1, by reporting the average between robust accuracy given by AutoAttack and the clean accuracy. Our conclusions remain unchanged in that uncertainty-based AT consistently brings better trade-offs relative to loss-based AT.
